title: Replacing Deprecated APIs
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of replacing deprecated apis and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—understanding deprecation warnings—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study replacing deprecated apis with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you evaluate upgrades using compatibility evidence instead of assuming every release feature is stable. In this lesson, focus on understanding deprecation warnings and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect understanding deprecation warnings with finding supported alternatives before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Understanding deprecation warnings
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

items.title: Finding supported alternatives
items.text: Java evolves across feature and LTS releases. Review official release notes, deprecations, API compatibility, and preview status before upgrading a project or adopting a new language feature. Apply that reasoning specifically to finding supported alternatives and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Testing replacements
items.text: A good test states the behavior it verifies and isolates the cause of a failure. Include boundary and error cases; coverage alone does not prove that assertions are meaningful.

items.title: Avoiding unnecessary compatibility breakage
items.text: Control flow decides which statements run and how often. Make conditions precise, set clear loop termination conditions, and test zero/one/many-item boundaries to catch off-by-one errors.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Compare source, binary, and behavioral compatibility, then run regression tests against the target JDK. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
